claims.text: The high-entropy alloy is initially a single-phase solid solution.
Processing with a controlled cooling rate will help preserve toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading.
Adding alloying elements that enhance solid-solution strengthening will help preserve toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading.
The intervention produces a stable solid solution.
The intervention produces a uniform distribution of alloying elements.
A stable solid solution with uniformly distributed alloying elements enhances alloy strength.
A stable solid solution with uniformly distributed alloying elements enhances alloy toughness.
Controlled cooling prevents the formation of unwanted phases or precipitates.
Unwanted phases or precipitates can degrade the alloy's mechanical properties.
Following thermal exposure and subsequent loading, the intervened alloy will have greater toughness than the comparator without the intervention.
Following thermal exposure and subsequent loading, the intervened alloy will have greater strength than the comparator without the intervention.
Without the intervention, the alloy will exhibit reduced toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading.
Without the intervention, the alloy will exhibit reduced strength after thermal exposure and subsequent loading.
High-entropy alloys can exhibit high strength, good ductility, and thermal stability.
Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has a simple solid-solution structure and favorable plasticity and machinability.
The optimal cooling rate and alloying elements are uncertain.

contradictions.description: The intervention includes adding alloying elements, which changes composition, yet the comparator is repeatedly called the 'same alloy' without the intervention. Unless the alloying-element intervention refers only to processing elements already present, the treated and untreated materials cannot literally be the same alloy.
